12 min read

Achieve legal equality




Global



































































What you’ll read:







Despite pushback, many are firmly committed to gender equality

: in a climate of global conflict and anti-rights pushback, we saw evidence of real progress, genuine political will and concrete support for gender-equal laws and policies.




Multilateralism matters more than ever, and it must include women

: alongside a UN Secretary General race featuring more women candidates than ever, we saw Member States leaning into, not away from, both multilateralism itself, and the idea that women are central to its success.




Everyone benefits from equality, and everyone has a part to play

: we know that whole societies reap the rewards of gender equality, but we also know that getting there requires all hands on deck. From intergenerational leadership to multisectoral coalitions and unexpected alliances, only by working and persevering together can we make equality reality.

After years of legislative setbacks, survivors and campaigners celebrate California setting the legal age of marriage at 18 years old without exception.




Sacramento, California, September

 30,

 2026 – 

California has finally banned child marriage. After nearly a decade of campaigning by 

Unchained At Last

 along with survivors, grassroots organizations, and human rights organizations such as 

Equality Now

, lawmakers have passed 

Bill AB-1267

, establishing 18 as the minimum legal age of marriage without exception. The law closes a longstanding loophole that allowed children of any age to marry with parental consent and judicial approval.




The victory is a milestone for girls’ rights and for advocates who watched reform efforts repeatedly falter for almost a decade.

title: Policy & Practice: How do we protect progress and keep advancing women’s rights?
content:
30th September 2026










Policy & Practice: How do we protect progress and keep advancing women’s rights?
















7 min read



















Policy & Practice




Achieve legal equality




Global


























































In the September issue of our Policy & Practice briefing, we share the latest insights from Equality Now and our partners’ expert teams worldwide. 




Around the world, women’s rights advocates continue to secure legal progress and defend hard-won protections, even as coordinated anti-rights movements seek to roll them back. From legal systems and political institutions to digital platforms and multilateral spaces, these movements are finding new ways to challenge gender equality.




So how do we protect the progress already made while continuing to advance the rights of women and girls?




Progress is not only possible, it’s happening




UN Women’s 2026 Gender Snapshot found that, at the current pace, 

gender equality is still 171 years away

. While these figures can be discouraging, our latest research shows that, even in an era that can sometimes feel defined by backlash, progress is not only possible; it’s happening.




To mark 31 years since the Beijing Declaration and Platform for Action, we released 

Words & Deeds: Strategically defending the rights of all women and girls in an era of backlash

.

Nepal’s flood recovery must address the heightened risks facing women and girls
















9 min read



















News and Insights




End harmful practices




Asia and the Pacific


























































Kathmandu, Nepal, September 26, 2026: 

On August 26, 2026, deadly flash floods and landslides ripped through Himalayan towns and villages along Nepal and Tibet’s border, devastating communities. T

he United Nations estimates that in Nepal’s worst-affected districts of Rasuwa and Nuwakot, 

157,050 women and girls are directly or indirectly impacted

.

 




As Nepal moves from emergency response to recovery and reconstruction, Ranjeeta Silwal, a human rights lawyer and Equality Now’s South Asia Regional Representative, explains in an interview how decisions about shelter, healthcare, education, livelihoods and social protection must prioritise the specific needs of women and girls. Ranjeeta, who lives in Kathmandu, calls for women and girls to have a central role in shaping recovery and climate adaptation, so rebuilding strengthens their rights and resilience rather than reinforcing existing gender inequalities.
